analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave program funded by a small payroll tax.
analysis.headline: A paid leave bill with 219 House cosponsors, including nearly every House Democrat, never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would give every working person paid time off — up to 60 caregiving days a year — for a new child, their own serious illness, or a seriously ill family member. Benefits would replace about two-thirds of a worker's monthly pay, between a floor of $580 and a cap of $4,000 a month, paid out of a new federal trust fund run through the Social Security Administration. It would be funded by a tax of 0.2% of wages on employees and the same on employers (self-employed people pay 0.4%). It would also make it illegal to fire or penalize a worker for using the benefit.
analysis.who_benefits: All working people, and especially those who today have no paid leave: the bill's findings note only 17% of civilian workers had employer-paid family leave, and just 5% of workers in the lowest-paying jobs. Low-wage workers, new parents, caregivers of elderly or ill relatives, and self-employed people would all qualify.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid leave, especially low-wage workers

how_it_helps.text: Every worker insured under Social Security rules could receive a benefit for up to 60 caregiving days per benefit period for a new child, their own serious health condition, or the serious health condition of a child, spouse, parent, or domestic partner.

The monthly benefit equals one-eighteenth of the worker's wages in their best of the last three years — roughly two-thirds of a typical month's pay — with a floor of $580 and a cap of $4,000 per month.

Funding comes from a dedicated tax of 0.2% of wages on employees and 0.2% on employers, with self-employed people paying 0.4%, deposited in a new Federal Family and Medical Leave Insurance Trust Fund separate from Social Security.
The bill makes it unlawful to discharge or discriminate against anyone who applies for or receives the benefit, and lets workers sue for lost wages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees.
It builds on the state programs in California, New Jersey, Rhode Island, New York and elsewhere, coordinating federal payments with state benefits rather than preempting them.

The bill's findings cite evidence from state programs that paid leave reduces nursing home use among the elderly, improves infant health and breastfeeding rates, and keeps workers attached to their jobs.

analysis.who_pays: Employees and employers each pay a new 0.2% payroll tax on all wages; a worker earning $50,000 and their employer would each pay about $100 a year. Self-employed people pay 0.4% on their income. Private short-term disability insurers would face a public program covering much of the same ground.
analysis.who_pays_short: All employers and workers, via payroll tax

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax falls on every wage dollar, so workers and employers who never take leave still pay; self-employed people pay double the employee rate on all self-employment income.
The benefit replaces only about two-thirds of a typical month's pay, and a five-day initial waiting period is not paid, so some households would still face a gap in the first week of leave.

The bill penalizes firing someone for applying for or receiving the benefit, but does not itself create a new right to job-protected leave; holding a job through leave still depends on existing law such as the Family and Medical Leave Act.

A universal program run through the Social Security Administration would be a significant new administrative undertaking, and the bill directs a Government Accountability Office study of processing delays three years after enactment — an acknowledgment that claims processing is a real risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad — a near-universal paid leave program — and the cost is modest and clearly labeled: a 0.4% combined payroll tax, roughly $1 in every $500 of wages. The strongest good-faith objections are the tax on people who never use the benefit, the reduced replacement rate for higher earners, and the fact that cash benefits are stronger than the job protection behind them. On balance it is a straightforward social insurance design, modeled on programs already operating in several states.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Worker and Family Support Subcommittee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the FAMILY Act in the House on February 13, 2019.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means and to the Subcommittee on Worker and Family Support.
The bill gathered 219 cosponsors — 218 of the 231 House Democrats and 1 of the 197 House Republicans — but that was the last recorded action on it.
The action history shows no subcommittee or committee vote, no floor debate, and no Senate companion action for the remainder of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers without paid leave gained nothing. Employers avoided the new 0.2% payroll tax, and private short-term disability insurers kept a market the public program would have partly displaced.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAMILY Act and recruited an original cosponsor list of more than 150 members.

for.name: 218 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the chairman of the committee it was assigned to.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: An original cosponsor of the bill, but as chairman never scheduled it for a committee markup or vote; it stayed in the Worker and Family Support Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 218 of 231 House Democrats versus 1 of 197 House Republicans cosponsoring — and because the bill never reached the floor, no roll-call votes were ever recorded on it.

industries.industry: Private short-term disability and paid-leave insurers
industries.note: The bill creates a public insurance benefit covering birth, illness, and caregiving — risks now sold as private short-term disability policies. A cheaper public alternative would compete directly with that market, so insurers benefit from the bill's failure.

industries.industry: Employers (all industries, especially low-wage service and retail)
industries.note: Employers pay a new 0.2% payroll tax, but state program evidence cited in the bill shows lower turnover and higher retention among low-wage workers. The industry's interest in avoiding the tax ran against the benefit to their own workers.
The bill leaves state programs in place and coordinates federal benefits with them rather than replacing them, so state-level systems keep their role.
